title: Houthis say they targeted Saudi capital with ballistic missiles
description: Iran-backed Houthi militants in Yemen say they carried out drone and ballistic missile attacks on the Saudi capital Riyadh, as well as energy sites on
body: Iran-backed Houthi militants in Yemen say they carried out drone and ballistic missile attacks on the Saudi capital Riyadh, as well as energy sites on the country's Red Sea coast.Saudi authorities said they intercepted and destroyed a ballistic missile fired at Riyadh earlier that day, without confirming any further strikes or causalities. Earlier, a column of black smoke was seen rising from fuel tanks near the Saudi capital's international airport, where flights were disrupted temporarily on Saturday. Air raid alerts had sounded in the capital for the first time since the Iran-backed Houthis increased their attacks on Saudi Arabia in July.Air defences also stopped "hostile attempts to target civilians" in the cities of Bish, Taif, Farasan and Yanbu, an official spokesperson for the Saudi-led coalition said in a statement.In a statement posted online, Houthi military spokesman Yahya al-Sarea said a "large number of ballistic and cruise missiles and drones" had been used to attack "sensitive sites" in Riyadh and Aramco state oil and gas company facilities in Yanbu on the coast.  He added that the attacks were "in response to the Saudi enemy's criminal attempts" to target the Yemeni capital Sanaa, which is currently controlled by the Houthis.Earlier, Sarea had accused Saudi Arabia of carrying out 300 strikes across Yemen during the past week.The Houthis are locked in a civil war with Yemen's internationally recognised government, which is backed by Saudi Arabia.They have attacked targets inside Saudi Arabia on several occasions in recent months, and said this week that they were responsible for downing a Saudi fighter jet over Yemen.According to an unconfirmed report from AFP news agency, quoting military sources on both sides of Yemen's civil war, fighting between the Houthis and Saudi-backed government forces claimed 48 lives on Saturday.The Houthis said 31 of their fighters had been killed while government sources said their side had lost 17 soldiers, according to the news agency.      On Friday, the International Organization for Migration, a UN body, reported that the number of people displaced as a result of recent fighting had passed 104,796, external.A number of apparent explosions were heard in Riyadh and major problems were reported at King Khalid International Airport earlier on Saturday, with the tracking website FlightRadar24 reporting delays and cancellations., externalAn AFP journalist reported that firefighters could be seen trying to extinguish the flames of a burnt-out fuel tank belonging to Aramco.The Saudi Civil Defence had sent out phone alerts overnight warning of potential danger in Riyadh and other regions, before issuing an all-clear on Saturday morning.Residents told AFP on condition of anonymity that they had heard what sounded like a round of explosions echoing through the city after the alerts."I heard the alarm, then my windows shook," said a resident of northern Riyadh, 27. "It was definitely scary. I was not expecting this."The Houthis recently seized control of the strategic port city of Mokha and Perim Island, a gateway to a key shipping route used by the Gulf state to export to Asia and Europe.The group said the naval blockade was in retaliation for a Saudi blockade of ports and airports in Houthi-controlled north-western Yemen.Saudi vessels have relied on that stretch of the Red Sea for oil exports since the US and Israel's war with Iran effectively closed the Strait of Hormuz.      On Friday, investment banking giant JP Morgan said it was struggling to predict how oil prices would be impacted by the war, telling investors in a rare note that "we simply don't know how to model the endgame".

schema.headline: Houthis say they targeted Saudi capital with ballistic missiles

title: Strictly is back with new hosts as celebrities discover pairings
description: Strictly Come Dancing has returned to the small screen for its 24th series, in a new era for the show as it moves forward with a revamped presenting l
body: Strictly Come Dancing has returned to the small screen for its 24th series, in a new era for the show as it moves forward with a revamped presenting line up.Broadcaster Emma Willis, comedian Josh Widdicombe and former Strictly professional Johannes Radebe made their presenting debut on Saturday, taking over from long-running hosting duo Tess Daly and Claudia Winkleman, who left the show last year.A fresh cohort of famous faces – including actress Melanie Walters and former England footballer Shaun Wright-Phillips – also stepped onto the ballroom floor for the first time.During the launch show, it was revealed which professional dancers they were paired with.Stepping out onto the ballroom floor after a huge all-cast opening dance routine, Willis said presenting Strictly was a "genuine honour". "Josh, you've got moves," proclaimed Radebe, a former professional on the show. While Widdicombe added that it was "a little bit overwhelming" but he was "delighted" to be there.In a first for the show, celebrity and pro pairings were revealed via three dance routines. It functioned as a musical chairs of sorts, in which the contestants switched partners until the music was paused, and a couple was announced. Here is a list of the pairings in full: Actress Lacey Turner and Vito CoppolaReality TV star Dani Dyer and Nikita KuzminHair stylist to the stars Chris Appleton and Amy DowdenAustralian singer and actress Delta Goodrem and Kai WiddringtonDJ and social media personality Cach Mercer and Maddie IngoldsbyTV and radio presenter Will Best and Dianne BuswellParalympian Dame Sarah Storey and Julian CaillonActress Jaime Winstone and Carlos GuTV and stage actress Bethany Antonia and Nancy XuFormer England footballer Shaun Wright-Phillips and Alexis WarrPresenter and author Graeme Hall and Lauren OakleyActor Lawrence Robb and Jowita PrzystałSkeleton athlete Tabby Stoecker and Mark KarmalitaYouTuber John Nellis and Katya JonesTV and stage actress Melanie Walters and Aljaž ŠkorjanecOne pair who won't need to get to know each other are reality TV star Dani Dyer and Nikita Kuzmin.Dyer is back to compete for a second time, having withdrawn from last year's series due to a fractured ankle."I'm just over the moon. I'm so, so happy," she said after the pairing, while Kuzmin added that he had "tears of joy" in his eyes. Meanwhile, actress Bethany Antonia and professional Nancy Xu became the third two-woman couple to compete in the show. In a poignant moment, Antonia revealed that watching boxer Nicola Adams and Katya Jones performing together in Strictly's 2020 series was a "big part of my coming out journey".Among the other pairings were EastEnders actress Lacey Turner and Vito Coppola, former Paralympian Dame Sarah Storey and Julian Caillon, and Shaun Wright-Phillips and Alexis Warr. Also back on the dancefloor for a final spin was reigning Strictly champion, former Lionness Karen Carney.Clad in the same diamante-encrusted football shirt, Carney recreated the Jive that first marked her out as a contender of her series, alongside dance partner Carlos Gu."I absolutely feel like I'm at home," Carney told Willis after the routine, as she paid tribute to her pro partner.  In 13 weeks time, she'll have to surrender that glitterball trophy to a new victor.

schema.headline: Strictly is back with new hosts as celebrities discover pairings

title: Earl Spencer's Diana book opens old wounds royals would rather forget
description: At issue is Earl Spencer's account of a conversation with the then Prince Charles after the death of Diana, with the prince accused of telling Earl Sp
body: At issue is Earl Spencer's account of a conversation with the then Prince Charles after the death of Diana, with the prince accused of telling Earl Spencer: "We'll forget her soon enough."He is accused of sounding "giddily elated" and like a "lottery winner" after the news of her death.Buckingham Palace hit back with a response, which although dressed in courtier-like politeness, was essentially saying the conversation had never happened like that.The King was said to be "mindful that the pain of fraternal grief can cloud reason, affect judgment and colour memory in ways that others do not recognise".Anyone who has lost someone knows how feelings can run high, people can hear different things about the same conversations - and families can fall out, or come together, in the wake of a death.Psychotherapist Nick Hatter says he doesn't have a view on which version of events is correct, but he says that during traumatic events memories can be "distorted". A phone call doesn't have any of the visual clues or body language to give a fuller picture, he adds.Hatter says there can be very different and unpredictable responses to grief, including a condition known as "bereavement mania" where someone can seem inappropriately hyper or even euphoric after the loss of a loved one.The first opinion poll on who to believe has been published by YouGov - and it suggests a very split view, with 31% believing Earl Spencer's allegations, 36% suspecting it's not true and 33% saying they don't know.Low thinks the book is unlikely to change many opinions, as "people have settled into their camps about how they regard Charles, how they look back on the Diana years".There could also be a feeling that it's "tawdry" to rake up these claims so many years later, he says.That's echoed by historian and author Sir Anthony Seldon who says Earl Spencer showed great courage at the time of Diana's funeral, but says his memoir is a "sad and unnecessary publication".Royal commentator Richard Palmer says the book threatens to take the royals back to the difficult days of 1997."This book and the run-up to next year's 30th anniversary of Diana's death threaten to undermine the Royal Household's three decades of work to rehabilitate Charles and Camilla's image," he says.Veteran broadcaster David Dimbleby, who led the BBC's coverage of Diana's funeral, said it seemed "odd" Earl Spencer would release the book now. "Why 30 years later for God's sake you should do it... you have to ask him,"  he said on Radio 4's Today programme, adding he wished the appetite for the "cycle of gossip" would decline and instead that focus would shift to what kind of monarchy the country needed. Earl Spencer, in a statement ahead of the book's launch, said he had been "inundated" with requests for interviews about his sister, with the upcoming 30th anniversary prompting him to write down his own memories "rather than having the discomfort of again reading the opinions of others, many of which are based on untruths that have become accepted over time". He is fiercely defending the accuracy of his claims, in interviews over the weekend, including with the BBC's Laura Kuenssberg.In it Earl Spencer doubles down on his allegations about King Charles, saying: "I can tell you here and now, those are exactly the words he said."I was hyper alert to what he was saying and those are precisely the words that he said and I promise that to you now. Genuinely, that is what he said. I don't hear him saying he didn't say that."

schema.headline: Earl Spencer's Diana book opens old wounds royals would rather forget

title: From fusty to fashionable - is it cool to wear M&S clothes now?
description: Image source, Carlo Paloni/Getty ImagesImage caption, M&S show during London Fashion Week September 2026ByAnnabel RackhamCulture reporterUpdated 11:52
body: Image source, Carlo Paloni/Getty ImagesImage caption, M&S show during London Fashion Week September 2026ByAnnabel RackhamCulture reporterUpdated 11:52 BST"I'm the first person to be like, 'It's from M&S, you need to get on to it,'" Farron Clark, a 26-year-old brand strategist tells me. According to Clark and others on social media, Marks & Spencer is becoming the hot place to shop for women under 35, while also keeping its core older audience happy too. "For a long time M&S had this fusty reputation - it was less valued by younger people," says Chioma Nnadi, head of editorial content at British Vogue, who tells the BBC there is now a "fresh energy around the brand".And accompanying that fresh energy is a new marketing strategy, which includes hosting its first-ever London Fashion Week show on Friday, featuring a collection of outfits inspired by the brand's archive.Image source, Reuters/Getty ImagesSpeaking ahead of the event at the Design Museum, the company's head of womenswear design, Lisa Illis, says they wanted to do this because of the "immediacy of seeing something and being able to own it and wear it, rather than waiting six months".For many, M&S is more synonymous with pig-shaped sweets than cutting-edge fashion, but its runway of 43 womenswear and 10 menswear looks did a lot to persuade people that the latter is where its true talent lies.Normally Fashion Week is about seeing what you'll be wearing six months from now, but this runway was full of colder weather fits, from opulent faux fur jackets and wrist cuffs, to satin jumpsuits and dresses in rich tones of navy, burgundy and brown.The catwalk featured a diverse range of models in age, size and gender, demonstrating the brand's desire to cater to a wide market. But there was certainly a concerted effort to attract the eye of younger shoppers with a fashion-forward approach to Christmas party staples like sequinned dresses, tasselled skirts and see-through lace tops.'They have created a modern version of everything we know and love'Image source, M&SImage caption, Womenswear and menswear collections at London Fashion Week are inspired by the M&S archiveThe retailer has been focusing on "newer styles and relevant trends" to attract younger customers, says Illis.But she says that this has been achieved without compromising on quality which is what keeps M&S's core audience on board."They have created a modern version of everything we know and love - cashmere staples, knitwear and the lingerie department," says Nnadi. Clark agrees that M&S has been nailing "funnel neck [styles] and barrel jeans, which are filtering down from high fashion".M&S has perhaps been fortunate to rebrand at a time when consumer habits are changing, as young shoppers consider buying capsule wardrobes - a smaller number of staple pieces that can be styled in a variety of ways. According to Clark, the idea of wear-it-once fast fashion has declined as people  "are looking for [foundational pieces] to rotate".This is something Perrie Sian, one of Britain's biggest fashion influencers, has also noticed. The 34-year-old tells the BBC: "The real height of fast fashion is behind us"."As a group we've changed our shopping habits and M&S slots into that," she says. "In my content and with lots of other creators we're showing people how to wear things in multiple ways, how to look after them."She added that she is noticing "people are willing to spend a little bit more" on wardrobe staples and items that "wash well and are made of cotton, not acrylic or polyester".Image source, Getty ImagesRevamped storesSpeaking on BBC Sounds podcast When It Hits The Fan, which she co-presents, Farzana Baduel, the president of the Chartered Institute of Public Relations, says it "hasn't always been rosy for M&S" and that past mis-steps had often led to the company being "absolutely hammered in the media"."M&S fashion, which for a while sat there like a bit of a sleepy Bagpuss on the British retail mantlepiece, has had quite a glow-up," Baduel says.During the Covid pandemic M&S struggled, but returned to growth in 2022-2023, with its fashion, home and beauty market share reaching 9.6%.This again increased in 2023-2024 to 10%, and 10.5% in 2024-2025.But the business took a big hit in 2025 due to a cyber attack, which left shoppers unable to use its website and app and affected stock in stores too.It means M&S's market share on fashion, home and beauty now sits at 10.2%, external for 2025-26.Nnadi says M&S has been investing heavily in its retail spaces in recent years, focusing on "accessible luxury" with stores that feel "welcoming, new and fresh".And that's something Clark has noticed too."Getting an iced coffee and having a walk around M&S with my friends is the perfect Saturday," she says. "My generation do so much sitting on our phones, so an in-person experience becomes a bit of an activity." Embracing young designers and collaborationsImage source, ReutersAccording to Sian, M&S has also taken "more risks" recently, which has helped it "create viral moments", including hosting a pit-lane fashion show at this year's F1 British Grand Prix and collaborating with British designers and creators."I'm seeing on Instagram or TikTok somebody say, 'Oh my goodness, this faux leather jacket is from M&S and it looks like it's £500 from the runway.' "And what am I doing? I'm hop, skip, jumping into my car and getting straight to my local M&S to hunt it down," Sian jokes. "They have embraced young designers like Marco Capaldo, the founder and creative director of 16Arlington," adds Nnadi. "And the Aries collab was genius and unexpected - it's a brand that has a lot of fashion kudos and is very British in its aesthetic but represents a younger vision of what British cool looks like," she says.Clark agrees the brand has "homed in on experts in their craft, rather than partnering with a million different people" like other fashion brands have made the mistake of doing.She notes their recent partnership with Stormzy's stylist Melissa Holbrook-Akposoe, who goes by Melissa's Wardrobe on social media, as "adding credibility" for younger shoppers.

schema.headline: From fusty to fashionable - is it cool to wear M&S clothes now?

title: An American found love at an Irish matchmaking festival - and hopes others do too
description: I found love at an Irish matchmaking festival - and I want others to do the sameFigure caption, "It was very serendipitous" - Mary and Jason on findin
body: I found love at an Irish matchmaking festival - and I want others to do the sameFigure caption, "It was very serendipitous" - Mary and Jason on finding love in IrelandBySheila FlynnSenior US ReporterMary Timby was fed up with dating apps when she booked a trip to Ireland on a whim last summer - from the comfort of her Colorado couch.The spur-of-the-moment trip was unlike her: Timby, 39, is a self-described "total planner". But she'd always wanted to visit Ireland, and she found herself exhausted by the local dating scene while navigating a career transition. And then she remembered a few throwaway lines from a comedy series about a matchmaking festival in Ireland.So she looked it up - and not only was the Lisdoonvarna Matchmaking Festival real, it was also taking place during the entire month of September, when she was scheduled to visit.Now, a little more than a year later, Timby is reaping the benefits of that uncharacteristic last-minute decision: She's become a viral star. She's found love with an Irishman she met at a pub called The Matchmaker. And she's even started a new business venture - bringing others to Lisdoonvarna who hope to follow in her footsteps.Image source, Mary TimbyImage caption, Timby and Jason Mangan, 38, from County Clare, Ireland, are pursuing a transatlantic romance"It's really about enjoying County Clare, enjoying the festival, and, if you meet someone, you do - and that's what happened with us," says Timby, smiling at her partner, Jason Mangan, sitting beside her.They're speaking from the windswept coastal cottage they rented together for the summer in his native County Clare - about 20 miles (32 km) southwest of Lisdoonvarna, the site of their first fortuitous meeting.'Mary, your video is going viral'From the outset, Timby's inaugural Ireland trip seemed to take on a life of its own.She filmed a short video on the plane before her flight took off, telling her approximately 300 TikTok followers that she was heading on an off-the-cuff trip to an Irish matchmaking festival - and didn't "know what's going to happen".Timby then "turned my phone on airplane mode, then spent about eight hours on the flight (and) woke up at Shannon Airport," she says.When she turned on her phone, "it was blowing up".A group of friends had texted her. "They said, 'Mary, your video is going viral,'" she says. "I didn't even have notifications on for social media."She rented a manual transmission car - horrified to find the gear stick on the left side of the driver's seat - and set off through County Clare to her accommodation at an Irish family's home. Then she headed to Lisdoonvarna, where she saw firsthand that the festival is a whole-town, month-long celebration of conversation and dancing, rather than a line of singles waiting to be set up by a sage local matchmaker.Image source, Mary TimbyImage caption, Colorado woman Mary Timby, 39, visited Ireland's Aran Islands with her new beauThat's changed since the festival's origins 170 years ago, when bachelor farmers and moneyed visitors would flock to the spa town of Lisdoonvarna to bathe in its mineral-rich waters and socialise. Generations of matchmakers would ply their trade to set up successful marriages, and word spread. Now, while the town's year-round residents number fewer than 1,000, up to 80,000 visitors descend upon Lisdoonvarna from around the world each September.Third-generation matchmaker Willie Daly still holds court at his nearby home and at festival events, and Timby even visited him during her trip - when he put her on the phone to random men whose accents she struggled to understand.But the real magic of contemporary Lisdoonvarna lies in the town's overflowing streets and pubs - as Timby soon found out.Her first night in town was "a little slow," she admits - and Timby was tired and jet-lagged. She retired to her room and spent the next day sightseeing, but the Irish woman running her accommodation convinced her to try Lisdoonvarna again that night."My AirBnB host said, 'You should go back tonight, because I heard that the younger folks come out at night,'" laughs Timby.So she did - and found herself dancing and drinking pints at The Matchmaker Bar in the centre of town. That's when a "handsome Irishman" approached her.'Conversation just flowed'"I went over and introduced myself, and... conversation just flowed," says Mangan, 38, from Ennis, County Clare, about 22 miles southeast of Lisdoonvarna. He'd been to the festival before and was well-acquainted with its cultural significance, remembering his grandparents making the journey decades earlier for the dancing."Unfortunately, I didn't have much time on my hands, because I was turning back to Ennis," says Mangan, designated driver that night for a group of friends. "So I got her name, and I said, 'Oh, sure, I might see you around.'"It was a very short interaction, to be honest with you."Image source, Mary TimbyImage caption, The couple first met at Lisdoonvarna's Matchmaker Bar during the annual festivalHe didn't leave it at that, though; Mangan found Timby on Instagram and followed up with a message inviting her out."It was short and sweet, and it was really genuine, too," says Timby - and she took him up on the offer.What followed was a series of whirlwind dates - lunches, dinners, sightseeing and shopping trips. Timby extended her time in Ireland and documented much of it for her newfound following - but she didn't reveal anything about her new beau. They wanted to save the burgeoning romance for themselves.When Timby eventually had to fly home, there were "tears at the airport" - but they decided to keep the relationship going."It was very tough to say goodbye," Timby says. "It was very tough to start a long-distance relationship, but it ended up being a really good opportunity for us to sort of slow things down a bit."They kept talking daily, Mangan impatiently waiting for Timby to wake up seven hours behind him in Colorado. She flew back to Ireland again, then he made his first trip to America for Thanksgiving 2025. Timby returned to Ireland at Christmas and met his family, and after that, they decided to make her boyfriend's big social media reveal."We thought, this is something we already know we want to invest in... we were ready to share," Timby says. "So New Year's Eve, we shared a photo of him, and people were just over-the-moon excited."The pair watched their following grow, drawing interest from Irish cafes and tourist destinations to the local Gaelic sports club in Colorado. Their story also caught the attention of Lisdoonvarna locals, who approached Timby - a communications consultant - about being an ambassador for the festival."So I said: Sign me up," Timby laughs. "I love the festival. It brought me Jay."Image source, Mary TimbyImage caption, Mangan has made repeated trips to Colorado since their 2025 meeting in IrelandTimby's been inundated with messages from lovelorn followers hoping to replicate her matchmaking success."I heard from many of my followers... groups of people wanting to go to the festival but not having anyone to go with" or "not knowing what to do," Timby says. "I really listened to that, and I also wanted to be mindful of the fact that I love Ireland."I'm so excited to showcase County Clare and all the amazing things that the west coast of Ireland has, but I'm also not a tour operator."So she partnered with a company called Met Through Friends, which organises and encourages real-life meetups for people looking for love. They released an interest form for a trip, expecting "80 to 100 responses." They received 560.The first group of eight will make the trip later this month, with Timby's Irish boyfriend consulting on the itinerary."You can go on all these apps, swipe left, swipe right, but it's not actually going out and making a connection with someone and experiencing a small little town in Ireland, experiencing the culture," says Mangan."It's a once-in-a-lifetime experience... you never know."Timby, smiling at her boyfriend of one year, agrees."I echo everything Jay just said," she says. "Put your phone down and put yourselves out there, and good things will come."

schema.headline: An American found love at an Irish matchmaking festival - and hopes others do too

title: Everton and Ipswich fans and players honour Noah Woods
description: Premier League fans and players honour Noah WoodsImage source, Action Images/ReutersImage caption, Ipswich and Everton fans stood to applaud in Noah's
body: Premier League fans and players honour Noah WoodsImage source, Action Images/ReutersImage caption, Ipswich and Everton fans stood to applaud in Noah's memory as a picture of him was shown on the big screenA tribute to three-year-old Noah Woods was shown on the big screen ahead of the Everton vs Ipswich Town Premier League match, while players wore black armbands in his memory.The toddler became separated from a relative after visiting a playground in Merriam Close, Brantham, on Tuesday afternoon, Suffolk Police said.About 1,300 members of the public joined a search to find Noah, who police said was non-verbal, partially deaf and had been undergoing an assessment for autism.Met Police divers recovered his body from a lake, known locally as Decoy Pond, on Wednesday afternoon and Suffolk Police said his death was not being treated as suspicious.Image source, Action Images/ReutersImage caption, Ipswich Town defender Leif Davis donated £2,000 to a fundraising appeal set up in aid of Noah Woods's familyThree minutes into the game, won 1-0 by the home side, both sets of supporters stood to applaud in memory of Noah, Everton said in a post on X, external.Town defender Leif Davis donated £2,000 to the fundraising appeal set up to support Noah's family and captain Dara O'Shea and goalkeeper Christian Walton were among the club delegation who laid flowers at the playground where he went missing.On Thursday, Noah's father Rhys Woods paid tribute to his son in a message shared on a community Facebook group.He wrote: "There are no words to describe the pain of this loss, we are all absolutely heartbroken, Noah was the sweetest and most innocent little boy, with nothing but love to give, and we are going to miss him so very much."Image source, Family handoutImage caption, Noah Woods was at a playground with a relative before he went missingSuffolk Police said on Thursday that the body of the child recovered by police divers had been formally identified as Noah, subject to confirmation at formal inquest proceedings.The force said police still have a number of inquiries to complete before submitting a file for the coroner.Meanwhile, a fundraising page set up by Good Dads Club, a community of fathers based in nearby Colchester, had received more than £100,000 in donations from a total of more than 6,000 supporters by Saturday evening.Do you have a story suggestion for Suffolk? Contact us below.Get in touchYour Voice

title: Lib Dems will be a firewall against Nigel Farage, Davey says
description: Sir Ed Davey said the Liberal Democrats are "a firewall against Nigel Farage and Reform" as the party's conference began in Brighton.The Lib Dem leade
body: Sir Ed Davey said the Liberal Democrats are "a firewall against Nigel Farage and Reform" as the party's conference began in Brighton.The Lib Dem leader sought to strike a combative stance as he faced down some criticism from MPs, including one who said publicly that they felt the party was struggling for relevance.On the first day of the autumn conference, Sir Ed warned an "unholy alliance" between Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch and Farage could turn the UK into a "Trump satellite state".Addressing speculation about a possible snap election, he said the party was ready to fight and would build its so-called orange wall even higher by winning more than its 2024 record of 72 MPs.Sir Ed's attention-grabbing stunts helped raise the party's profile ahead of the last election, but recent polling showed 43% of respondents were unclear what the Liberal Democrats stand for, with just over half describing them as "weak".In an essay, external written ahead of conference, South Cotswolds MP Roz Savage asked: "Why are we as a party struggling for relevance at precisely the moment when so many people feel powerless?"She urged the party to rediscover its "insurgent spirit" rather than being the "polite custodians of a system that leaves people feeling powerless".Asked about her comments, Sir Ed said: "No, I heard Roz [Savage], and I really value her, but I think she's wrong on that. "If you look at our election results up and down the country, we now run more councils than the Conservatives."He added: "Listen, MPs get elected and they get frustrated because they can't change the world."I'm afraid that's the political system. I've been used to it for a little while and people are learning about that frustration."Speaking on the pebbles of Brighton Beach, Sir Ed told reporters the Liberal Democrats would fight to stop a Reform government."One of the things that makes us unique is that we are a firewall against Nigel Farage and Reform," he said."Many of the seats he needs to get himself into No 10 are seats that we will defend and indeed win - and we are also able to take seats off the Conservatives, because I really fear that Kemi Badenoch will give the keys to No 10 to Nigel Farage, so we have got to stop the Conservatives as well."We have got an historic opportunity to win many more seats and a moral responsibility to stop Reform."He added a manifesto working group had already been set up in case of an early election "so we'll be ready if it comes early, but, you know, it still could be up to three years away". Sir Ed insisted his party has a "distinctive position" in British politics, and will use the four-day conference to position it to take on the challenge from Reform as well as its typical rivals the Conservatives, talking up their focus on the NHS and goal of re-joining the EU single market and customs union. The Lib Dem leader highlighted how six former Conservative cabinet ministers were among 25 Tories to have defected to Reform in the last two years, claiming they were now competing with each other to see who can divide the country more, rather than looking to fix the country's problems."An unholy alliance between Farage and Badenoch is the only way either can get into power," he said."Together, they want to turn Britain into a Trump satellite state which would trash our NHS, turn our communities against each other, cause untold damage to our environment, and trample over traditional British values of fairness, tolerance, and decency."A bigger Orange Wall is the only thing that can stand between Britain and this dangerous experiment, and we will not let them pass."Davey also attacked the Labour government as having no plan for growth, failing to support families struggling with the cost of living and taxing small businesses "to the brink".Ahead of a speech to party members, Davey urged Liberal Democrats not to look away from injustice or "human dignity under attack" but to fight back.

schema.headline: Lib Dems will be a firewall against Nigel Farage, Davey says

title: US and Denmark reach deal over Greenland's security after Trump threats
description: The US and Denmark have announced a deal on Greenland's security, resolving a diplomatic dispute sparked by President Donald Trump's threats to seize
body: The US and Denmark have announced a deal on Greenland's security, resolving a diplomatic dispute sparked by President Donald Trump's threats to seize it by force.Nato said the deal would help stabilise the region, as Trump said Denmark would grant the US "permanent control over security, and all other needs" in the semi-autonomous Danish territory.The leaders of Denmark and Greenland welcomed the deal to "strengthen security", which they said was expected to be signed next week, but did not outline its contents.The deal comes after months of threats by Trump to "take" Greenland over national security concerns, citing its strategic location for defence purposes and its mineral wealth.No text of the agreement has been released. Trump said the deal came with "no cost to the United States" and would grant it the ability "to do what is necessary" to "secure and defend the security of Greenland", in a post on Truth Social.He said it included a rule that no US adversary could maintain a military presence in Greenland or "make sensitive investments in Greenland, without our express written approval".A Nato spokesperson said the military alliance welcomed the deal, which would "help advance security, stability and cooperation in this vital region".Denmark's Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen said she was "pleased that there is a prospect of a good agreement" for all three parties, which was expected to be signed at the UN General Assembly next week.The deal "strengthens our common security in the Arctic and the North Atlantic area" while also recognising "the sovereignty and territorial integrity of the Kingdom and the right of the Greenlandic people to self-determination", she said in a joint statement with Greenland's Prime Minister Jens-Frederik Nielsen.The agreement would still need to go through "the necessary parliamentary procedures to enter into force" once signed, the statement noted.Nielsen said it was "gratifying that we are about to enter into an agreement that ensures and strengthens the security of Greenland, the Kingdom of Denmark, the United States and the Western alliance"."The agreement recognises Greenland's interests and our place in international co-operation. It is for the benefit of us all," he said.Trump had tried for months to purchase or annex the semi-autonomous territory, arguing that it was vulnerable to adversaries, including Russia and China. His repeated demands to take Greenland earlier this year prompted an outcry from Greenlanders, Danes and other Nato members.There is hope the crisis has now been brought to an end, with some Danish media interpreting the agreement as a quiet but significant triumph for the country's diplomacy."Don't tell Trump that it's the Kingdom of Denmark that has won," read one headline in the newspaper Berlingske on Saturday."Trump didn't get Greenland, but he was allowed to take a victory lap on social media," wrote a US correspondent for Politiken. Territorial integrity was a red line for Denmark and Greenland, and the US president has made no mention of any territory changing hands.It is not yet clear what concessions or sweeteners, if any, have been agreed - and in Greenland, some are still nervous."[It's] news we have all been hoping for," MP Naaja Nathanielsen wrote on social media. But she added: "It is absolutely crucial that any agreement preserves our right to self-determination."Former Greenlandic politician Aaja Chemnitz said she looked forward to the deal being finalised, but "until then, I'm sceptical". "I don't have much confidence in Trump," she said.The text of the agreement has not been published. The BBC has contacted the Danish Embassy in the US and the White House.However, an unnamed US State Department official outlined the deal without providing specifics.Among the agreed provisions is one stating the deal would not expire even if Greenland became an independent country in the future.The official added that under the deal, the US has unilateral power to build additional military structures with no approval needed from Greenland or Denmark. It includes "permanent access, basing and overflights rights," the official said.It also bans non-Nato countries from building bases in Greenland, and "bans adversaries from making investments in Greenland that could threaten the United States".The official added that under the current status quo, adversaries have been allowed to invest in Greenland's "sensitive sectors without investment screening".The official specifically referenced Russia and China, saying it blocks them from deploying troops or making investments in "sensitive sectors".

schema.headline: US and Denmark reach deal over Greenland's security after Trump threats

title: Fire Folkestone's Grand Burstin Hotel treated as suspicious
description: Major seaside hotel fire treated as suspiciousImage source, Dave HennessyImage caption, A seaside hotel in Folkestone has been evacuated after a fire
body: Major seaside hotel fire treated as suspiciousImage source, Dave HennessyImage caption, A seaside hotel in Folkestone has been evacuated after a fire in the early hoursByChrissie ReidyReporting fromin FolkestonePatrick Barlow and Hsin-Yi LoSouth EastUpdated 1 hour agoA fire at a seaside hotel where about 280 people were evacuated is believed to have been caused deliberately, police have said.A total of 26 fire engines were sent to the Grand Burstin Hotel in Folkestone at about 01:05 BST on Saturday, Kent Fire & Rescue Service said. Kent Police said that the fire was being treated as suspicious and is appealing for witnesses."Inquiries into the circumstances are under way," police said. Image source, Juliette FeltonImage caption, Kent Police is appealing for witnesses to the hotel fireIn an update at 20:35, the fire service said that three fire engines and a height vehicle remained in attendance, and firefighting operations were ongoing.Crews will stay in attendance overnight to monitor and extinguish any remaining hotspots, it said. "An investigation is under way to establish the cause of the fire at the Grand Burstin Hotel in Folkestone, which is being treated as suspicious," a fire service spokesperson said.Station manager Lawrence Pater said the "very severe" fire had raised concerns about the structural integrity of the building, and that it was seeking advice from inspectors.Image source, Kent Fire & Rescue ServiceImage caption, At the height of the incident, a total of 26 fire engines were at the sceneFolkestone & Hythe District Council has set up a welfare centre at the Three Hills Sports Park, and nearby residents have been advised to avoid the area of the fire and close windows and doors."We are supporting all emergency services involved in the response and their efforts to get people to safety", the council said. South East Coast Ambulance Service said it assessed a number of people at the scene and one person was taken to hospital with minor injuries.A spokesperson for Britannia Hotels Group, which runs the Grand Burstin Hotel, said it was "taking immediate action to ensure the safety and wellbeing of all guests and team members"."Emergency services are on site and we are fully cooperating with the authorities to support those affected and assist with the ongoing response", it added.Image source, Chrissie Reidy / BBCImage caption, Ross Honeycomb was evacuated from the hotel with his familyRoss Honeycomb, 39, was staying at the hotel with his family and told the BBC that they were woken by fire alarms at about 01:00.He said: "I thought I was dreaming, it was horrifying."We looked out and there was smoke billowing from the underground car park. Later we started hearing explosions.""It has just been madness. I have been out barefoot all night."Bill Owen, who checked in on Saturday afternoon, said that when he walked past the car park, the "heat coming out of it was incredible".He added: "We could see thick black smoke. You could taste it."Another person told BBC South East that the fire had been "wind driven" and had begun in the basement, though a cause of the fire had not yet been established.Image source, Chrissie Reidy/BBCImage caption, Kevin and Kathleen said that they felt "lucky to be alive" after the fireKevin Crawford, 91, and his wife Kathleen, 82, said that they had booked in for a two-week stay at the hotel. The couple, from London, told the BBC that they were in their room on the sixth floor when they heard a fire alarm. "We saw the fire but we thought the fire brigade had it under control," Kevin Crawford said."We managed to sleep through it. At the time, we didn't realise how bad the fire was."HIs wife said that they were brought down from their room after waving to people from the window."The hotel is very damaged," she added. "We are so lucky to be alive."Image source, Chrissie Reidy/BBCImage caption, Ben Cuthbert, owner of The Harbour Inn, opened his restaurant to give evacuees a place to restBen Cuthbert, owner of The Harbour Inn, opened his restaurant for those who evacuated."I got a call in the middle of the night and I was told there was a big fire at the hotel," he said. Cuthbert added that there were many people who did not know where to go or what to do."Some people left their room only in their night gowns and had nothing else with them," he said. "A lot of people were scared, we helped comfort them by giving them a place to rest."Cuthbert also offered space for paramedics to treat people. Kent Police said that officers were called to the hotel at about 01:20 to "assist traffic flow" while firefighters tackled the blaze.Kent County Council leader Linden Kemkaran paid tribute to emergency services on X, saying firefighters responded "rapidly, professionally and with saving lives at the forefront of their minds".Follow BBC Kent on Facebook, external, on X, external, on Instagram, external and listen to BBC Radio Kent on Sounds. Send your story ideas to southeasttoday@bbc.co.uk, external or WhatsApp us on 08081 002250.

schema.headline: Fire Folkestone's Grand Burstin Hotel treated as suspicious

title: CNN, MS NOW and Politico say reporters denied White House access after Trump banned some media outlets
description: "The officer asked me to hand over my badge. He said that it was disabled," MS NOW reporter Akayla Gardner said. "I asked why I was not able to get in
body: "The officer asked me to hand over my badge. He said that it was disabled," MS NOW reporter Akayla Gardner said. "I asked why I was not able to get inside. He said it was above him."Gardner added that while her and her colleague's badges were disabled, an MS NOW producer was still able to scan her badge to get in, though she was not given an explanation as to why the producer's badge still worked.CNN reporter Betsy Klein said a Secret Service agent told her her badge had been deactivated.Later on Saturday morning, Politico said its reporter Cheyenne Haslett was denied entry and Secret Service revoked her pass. All three outlets have spoken out against the decision, accusing Trump of violating their constitutional rights to free speech and freedom of the press.An MS NOW spokesperson said in a statement that the White House "belongs to the American people and the decisions made inside are funded by our tax dollars".MS NOW said it "intends to take any and all steps necessary to defend our First Amendment rights and the essential role of independent journalism in our democracy".Politico Editor-in-Chief Jonathan Greenberger said in an internal email, shared in the outlet's Playbook newsletter, that the company stands by its reporters and will "vigorously defend" their First Amendment rights. And CNN said, "We have a right under the US Constitution to do our reporting without hindrance or interference from the government and this ban is an illegal assault on this fundamental right."In his announcement, Trump did not mention specific stories or reporting from the three outlets that prompted the move, but later said "it's really just cumulative stories over the last few years".Trump added that there "may be others to join them", but has not given a directive banning additional news outlets. When later asked by a reporter what he meant by others to come, Trump responded: "Others to come in terms of fake news? Well, you know, the New York Times is fake news, the Washington Post is fake news."The White House Correspondents Association (WHCA) - the independent, non-profit group that represents journalists who cover the US presidency - called on the administration "to immediately restore" access to the journalists and accused it of violating the First Amendment. "The implications extend beyond these organizations: a standard used to exclude one news outlet because of its coverage could be applied to any outlet in the future," said WHCA President Jacqui Heinrich, who works for Fox News.Heinrich said that the Americans, through a free and independent press, must be able to scrutinise those elected in their coverage "regardless of whether government officials view it favorably"."That's why courts have repeatedly held that once the White House provides access to journalists, it cannot deny that access arbitrarily or based on the content of their reporting."Several groups dedicated to the freedom of the press have called Trump's White House ban illegal and unconstitutional.A major group that provides legal services to the media - the Reporters Committee for Freedom of the Press - said it expected Trump's ban to be struck down quickly by the courts because it was "flatly unconstitutional"."The First Amendment is clear that once the White House invites in some journalists, it can't ban others because it doesn't like their reporting," said Bruce Brown, president of the Reporters Committee for Freedom of the Press, which provides legal services to the media.It's the latest in a series of moves by the administration to target media outlets Trump says are critical of him, including legal action against US and international outlets like The New York Times, The Wall Street Journal, and the BBC.Some of the lawsuits have resulted in media organisations agreeing to pay multimillion dollar settlements. Trump's lawsuit against the BBC is ongoing.Additional reporting from Bernd Debusmann Jr and Max Matza.

schema.headline: CNN, MS NOW and Politico say reporters denied White House access after Trump banned some media outlets

title: Trump ramps up feud with press after week of setbacks
description: The president's frustration at the media, however, came after a week of setbacks in which major institutions handed him a series of losses across his
body: The president's frustration at the media, however, came after a week of setbacks in which major institutions handed him a series of losses across his agenda.First, the Supreme Court blocked his plan to restrict mail-in voting ahead of the midterms. This prompted Trump to lash out at the court's justices including those he had appointed. "These are not the people I interviewed to serve on the United States Supreme Court," he said.The Federal Reserve, the US central bank, then raised interest rates after Trump had spent months arguing they should be cut. This was followed by a judge ordering his administration to give 30 days' notice before making any changes to the Kennedy Center arts venue in Washington DC after the president warned it could be "ripped down".These headlines, combined with approval ratings that recently sunk to record lows for his second term, suggest Trump is facing challenging political headwinds.His latest attack on the press, however, raises clear legal questions. The First Amendment to the US Constitution forbids Congress from "abridging" the freedom of the press. It is language that courts have long interpreted as preventing the government from discriminating against the media based on the content of their coverage.All three targeted news outlets have promised to file lawsuits challenging Trump's decision.Although the breadth of this move is unprecedented, it is far from the first time the Trump administration has attempted to limit or deny access to the White House to members of mainstream media outlets.In his first term, the administration revoked CNN correspondent Jim Acosta's press credentials, setting off a legal battle that was ultimately resolved in the journalist's favour. It also temporarily suspended the pass of a reporter who had a heated argument with White House adviser Sebastian Gorka – a move that also was subsequently blocked by the courts.Last year, the White House banned reporters for the Associated Press from participating in the president's press pool - which allows media outlets access to smaller in-town and travelling presidential appearances - because the newswire service would not follow Trump's move to rename the Gulf of Mexico as the Gulf of America.That dispute also led to a protracted - and yet to be fully resolved - legal battle, prompting the White House to change press pool rules to drop the guaranteed spot for all wire services.The White House bans, however, represent a dramatic escalation. The restrictions include access to the entirety of the White House grounds, not just the press pool. And they target entire news organisations, not just a single disfavoured correspondent.While Trump has been clear about the motives behind his decision, he has shed little light on why he has acted now. He has regularly criticised his press coverage since he first entered national politics more than a decade ago, but he said on Friday there was no specific incident that prompted his announcement.At the moment, however, the president is embattled. Even beyond the week of clear setbacks, he is in the midst of an unpopular and difficult-to-resolve war of choice in Iran, which has led to a surge in energy and other consumer prices, deflating his standing with the American public.Polls also suggest his party faces an uphill battle to retain control of the House of Representatives and perhaps the Senate in November's crucial midterm congressional elections.His attempts to improve the public's mood by touting his accomplishments in campaign events and at his Republican Party's convention earlier this month in Texas have, at least so far, proven ineffective.There may be more behind Trump's decision to lash out at the media this weekend. But it could also simply be an indication of presidential frustration in the face of events and circumstances, some of his own making, that are turning against him.

schema.headline: Trump ramps up feud with press after week of setbacks

title: Ekurhuleni killings: Grim discoveries of murdered women spark fear in South Africa
description: "What we are going to do, I have no idea," sobs Nokwanda Matshikiza, reflecting on the murder of her niece Dineo Motapane. "But something must give.""
body: "What we are going to do, I have no idea," sobs Nokwanda Matshikiza, reflecting on the murder of her niece Dineo Motapane. "But something must give.""For us, for all the other women. How many other bodies will be found before something happens?"Nokwanda is speaking to the BBC from the family home near South Africa's main city, Johannesburg, just two days after relatives identified Dineo's body.The 38-year-old mother-of-two was last seen alive on Sunday. Her battered and partly burned body was later found in the residential region of Ekurhuleni.Nokwanda weeps as she describes how the family will have to face, at some point, the grim task of telling Dineo's daughter of her death."How do you explain that your parent was brutally murdered, dumped in a field, and just left there, discarded like a piece of rubbish."There's no coming to peace with it," she adds. "It's something that you can never reconcile yourself with, that you can never get over."Dineo's death this week has come amid a series of comparable incidents in Ekurhuleni – her body one of three discovered there this week. In total, nine bodies of murdered women have been found in similar circumstances in the region since July.The problem has always been there but this spate of grim discoveries has once again sparked a national outcry about the scale of violence against women in the country – which has one of the highest rates of gender-based violence in the world.Themba Kekana is also living in shock at the death of a loved one.His sister, Itumeleng, was one of the first to disappear in Ekurhuleni.The 32-year-old shopkeeper's body was found in July, 17 days after she was last seen alive. Her body was badly bruised, partially clothed and dumped on a bridge."We are devastated with grief," says Themba, wet eyes shining."I look at my sister's young daughter and my eyes fill with tears, I know there is no way that I can ever take this pain away from her."No family should have to deal with what we are faced with."Only one arrest has been made in connection with the murders – and that was two days after the first body was discovered on 15 July.Nobody has been detained following the murders of Itumeleng or Dineo or the other six Ekurhuleni women.Most of the victims were young, in their 20s or 30s, and almost all had suffered extreme violence before their deaths.Police have said they are not sure if they are hunting a serial killer. It is possible the cases are not linked.Either way, what has happened in this residential district east of South Africa's biggest city has traumatised the nation, shining a spotlight on a situation that many believe is a crisis.South Africa's police issue detailed crime statistics every quarter, which show that between April and June this year - 5,427 people were murdered.The official data does not distinguish between the genders of the victims, but this week the country's Human Rights Commission released figures showing that 569 women had been killed in that period (six a day on average), with another 1,052 who faced attempted murder.Many women - already feeling unsafe - have been left reeling by recent events.And it has put pressure on the government, less than a year after ministers acknowledged the scale of the issue and declared gender-based violence a national disaster.Announcing the move last November, Minister of Social Development Nokuzola Sisisi Tolashe said that treating the issue as a national disaster would help the government tackle the crisis.It followed weeks of protests, culminating in a "Women's Shut Down" march as South Africa hosted the G20 summit.This week has seen a chorus of calls for things to go further.Rights group Amnesty International said an important first step towards protecting South Africa's women was to recognise femicide as a separate crime."Every day that femicide remains unrecognised as a crime is a failure to confront the targeted killing of women," said Amnesty's country director Shenilla Mohamed in a statement. "It is time to call it what it is: Femicide."Femicide is a gender-motivated crime. It is the killing of a woman because she is a woman."Amnesty says femicide is criminalised as a specific crime in 33 countries, including Gabon and Morocco in Africa.It argues that making that change in South Africa could help focus on the scale of the issue."It would compel the state to confront their failure to protect women and girls from violence," says Mohamed. "You cannot fix what you are not tracking."Almost everyone in South Africa agrees more needs to be done.President Cyril Ramaphosa this week pledged to leave "no stone unturned" in investigating the crimes in Ekurhuleni, adding: "As a nation, we must stand up for the rights, safety and dignity of women and girls."Lebogang Ramafoko, an advocate for gender and social justice, said the levels of violence against women in the country were symptomatic of a much bigger problem – a lack of regard for humanity."The bodies of black women have been treated as disposable in this country for time immemorial, passed down from colonisation through to apartheid," she tells the BBC, referring to the legalised system of racism that was in place until 1994."What we see happening to women is testimony to legacies of violence from those systems whose traumas were never addressed."This is not to say black men are inherently violent, but in systems where violence was meted out against them for decades, historically black women were the people that that violence would be taken out on - that cycle has not been broken."In Kempton Park, a district of Ekurhuleni where five of the nine recent bodies were found, Lumka Maqhubela is part of the Girl2Woman Foundation group which has held protests to raise awareness of the crimes."We are grieved, we are scared," she says. "If the police cannot protect us any more the government should step in and do something."It's clear that we are not safe, we cannot be told by the police to be more vigilant. They should be doing more to make our communities safe – what else are we expected to do? We are not safe anywhere, not in our homes, not in the streets, it needs to stop.""I feel uncomfortable," says Thulisile Sibande, 32. "When I go to a shop, I have to look around. I'm shocked and scared. So scared, it's a trauma."Thembi Mabena, 60, tells the BBC she lived in the same neighbourhood as Dineo Motapane."She was laughing every day, with everybody," she remembers. "Now I'm worried."I know many children, girls, who tell me they are afraid to go to the shop alone. There is no safety, even for me too. I am old, but there is no safety.""In South Africa," says Lerato Mzizi, 20, simply, "women are not safe any more."

schema.headline: Ekurhuleni killings: Grim discoveries of murdered women spark fear in South Africa

title: Daisy Edgar-Jones: I'm like my character in Sense and Sensibility
description: Daisy Edgar-Jones: I try and bury my emotion when it comes to loveImage source, Getty ImagesByNoor NanjiCulture correspondentDaisy Edgar-Jones has bee
body: Daisy Edgar-Jones: I try and bury my emotion when it comes to loveImage source, Getty ImagesByNoor NanjiCulture correspondentDaisy Edgar-Jones has been well cast in her new film.She plays Elinor, the rational elder sister in Sense and Sensibility, opposite the younger, more romantic sister Marianne.Speaking to the BBC, Edgar-Jones says that in her personal life, she really is like her character."When it comes to love, I think I am very much more Elinor in every sort of way," she says."I definitely lead a lot with my head and try and push aside, bury my emotion."But she notes that one of the joys of the film is seeing Elinor learn to enjoy a "wilder, passionate side" of herself. "And I feel like I learnt to do that too," she says.Best known for starring in hit TV series Normal People with Paul Mescal, Edgar-Jones, 28, is now taking on a lead role in the latest adaptation of Jane Austen's book.Ahead of its release, she’s been talking to me about whether we really need another Sense and Sensibility film (spoiler: yes. “The more the merrier, in my opinion.”)She also told me why young people today can still see themselves in Jane Austen's stories - and gave me her take on whether her friend and former co-star Mescal should be the next James Bond. Image source, Alex Bailey / 2026 FOCUS FEATURES LLCImage caption, Daisy Edgar-Jones and Esmé Creed-Miles in a scene from Sense and SensibilityThe new film, directed by Georgia Oakley, follows the Dashwood sisters as they navigate their way through love, loss and societal expectations, following the death of their father.It's a classic adaptation of Austen's novel, rather than a more contemporary take.When I meet Edgar-Jones at a hotel in central London, I ask her whether there was ever a temptation to make it more "2026"."It does feel very much like it's honouring the period," she agrees, "but I think there's a freshness to the filmmaking that I think is really beautiful".She is starring alongside Esmé Creed-Miles, 26, who plays her sister Marianne.Together, the two sisters' different approaches to life are characterised as "sense" (Elinor) and "sensibility" (Marianne).Creed-Miles is also well cast, it seems. "I'm more like Marianne [than Elinor], yeah, which is annoying sometimes," she laughs.Image source, Alex Bailey / 2026 FOCUS FEATURES LLCImage caption, Daisy Edgar-Jones stars as Elinor in Sense and SensibilitySense and Sensibility has been adapted for screen countless times before - including the hit 1995 film starring Emma Thompson and Kate Winslet.Edgar-Jones loves that version (“one of my favourite films of all time”) but also feels there's room to tell Austen’s classic tale again."Her stories are something that fascinate us still today,” she says.It was also easy for her and Creed-Miles to build the sisterly rapport on screen, as they previously worked together as teenagers on the 2018 film Pond Life.“We had a real laugh," Creed-Miles says of their time on that film. "We would have sleepovers every night and watch Love Island."For Edgar-Jones, the theme of sisterhood is something that stuck with her from Sense and Sensibility - despite her being an only child in real life.“I've heard a lot of people say that after watching the film, it either makes them want a sister or to ring up their sister and say like, ‘Hey, I love you,’ and I think that's really special. It's the part of the film I'm most proud of.”Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Esmé Creed-Miles and Daisy Edgar-Jones play two sisters in Sense & SensibilityJane Austen seems to be everywhere right now.Last year marked the 250th anniversary of her birth and, in recent years, we've enjoyed two BBC TV series, Miss Austen and The Other Bennet Sister, the West End's Clueless musical (based on the cult 90s teen film adaptation of Emma), and Ava Pickett's modern stage adaptation of Emma.There's also a new adaptation of Pride and Prejudice written by Dolly Alderton and starring Emma Corrin coming to Netflix.For Edgar-Jones, the themes in Austen's books are just as revelant today."She has an incredible way of articulating the female experience," she says."Her ruminations on love, on romance, on sisterly love, on family dynamics, on interpersonal social dynamics - she's such a talent."Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Daisy Edgar-Jones takes a selfie with a fan at the world premiere for Sense and Sensibility in London earlier this weekAusten also wrote about the sort of dating behaviour that people complain about on TikTok (like situationships and ghosting), before terms like that had even been invented. Does that help Gen Z audiences relate to her, I ask?"Well, massively," replies Edgar-Jones."We still have the same human heart as we did 200 years ago. Our capacity to love and feel heartbreak, and that early first love feeling, is something that we all experience in various ways."And so yes, I think definitely the trials and tribulations of the two women [Elinor and Marianne] as they navigate life, love and all that becomes as you grow up, definitely is so relatable to all generations.""These women are very relatable," agrees Creed-Miles."I don't know if seeing a movie is going to fix everything, but it might make you feel a little bit less alone in some of the things you're feeling."Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Daisy Edgar-Jones and Paul Mescal's breakout roles were in Normal People, which came out in 2020Edgar-Jones shot to fame during the pandemic with her role in Normal People.Based on Sally Rooney's novel, the BBC Three drama charted the on-off relationship of teenagers Marianne and Connell, played by Edgar-Jones and Paul Mescal.The pair have remained close (a few years ago, Edgar-Jones told me Mescal was "one of my all-time best friends") - and both are now successful actors. Edgar-Jones has since starred in Twisters and Where The Crawdads Sing, while Mescal was in Gladiator II, Hamnet and will be in the Beatles films.Recently, Page Six claimed Mescal was on the audition list to be the next James Bond, external.So, is he really in the running? Edgar-Jones didn’t give too much away.“I don’t know, but I think there’s nothing Paul can’t do,” she says.“So I would be there. Wow, that’s cool.”Sense and Sensibility is out in UK cinemas on 25 September.

schema.headline: Daisy Edgar-Jones: I'm like my character in Sense and Sensibility

title: Celtic win over Rangers 'changes game', says Scott Brown before Old Firm derby
description: With Yang Hyun-jun still on Asian Games duty with South Korea, Sebastian Tounekti and James Forrest have both been used on Celtic's left flank.But Bro
body: With Yang Hyun-jun still on Asian Games duty with South Korea, Sebastian Tounekti and James Forrest have both been used on Celtic's left flank.But Brown believes the club's problems go beyond that. "Rangers got in their face, they blocked Callum McGregor off and as soon as you block Callum McGregor off and you man-mark Cal, it's hard for anyone else to go and dictate."That's when you need a [Benjamin] Nygren to drop under, a [Mika] Baur to go and drop under and them do their job as well. You can't always keep looking at Cal to do everything."And Brown believes who starts best could be crucial."Rangers were up for the fight," he added on Sportsound. "The first 15 minutes, it should be a battle. If you can go and win that battle, you can get the ball down."Celtic started very, very slow last week. They need to go back to basics, make sure they've got the fight, make sure they've got the hunger because they've got the talent - I know they've got the talent."You cannot have just one of those days against your biggest rivals, ever."

schema.headline: Celtic win over Rangers 'changes game', says Scott Brown before Old Firm derby

title: When a beloved tree began withering away, locals suspected a killer in their midst
description: ByYujin ChoiBBC KoreanReporting fromSeoul and Koh EweEvery summer, Seoul turns a deep green, growing dense and lush under humid skies.But this year, o
body: ByYujin ChoiBBC KoreanReporting fromSeoul and Koh EweEvery summer, Seoul turns a deep green, growing dense and lush under humid skies.But this year, one tree was visibly suffering. "Green leaves were falling to the ground, which shouldn't happen at that time of year," recalls Jung, who lives near the streetside ginkgo in Buam-dong, a largely residential neighbourhood in the north of Seoul.The tree is beloved by locals, who believe it has occupied its spot for more than 100 years. So Jung couldn't ignore what she was seeing. With each passing day, her curiosity turned to concern.A rotting carpet of familiar fan-shaped leaves soon surrounded the tree, a sight so alarming Jung and her neighbours formed a crew of amateur detectives to solve the mystery: what was ailing their hardy ginkgo?The whodunnit engrossed Buam-dong and piqued the country's interest, making national headlines. But the attention unsettled Jung, who spearheaded the campaign but has since requested anonymity - we are using a pseudonym."Imagine a grandfather who silently embraces you every day, listens to you, and has always been strong and full of life," she says. "Suddenly, he begins to die. "How heartbreaking would that be?"So began one community's fight to save a cherished symbol of their neighbourhood. Their unlikely enemy, who they believe plotted a surreptitious attack, was a museum built to honour a pioneering, nature-loving Korean artist.Image source, Yujin Choi/BBCImage caption, As summer went by, the ginkgo's branches started to turn bare and brownWho is killing 'Grandpa Ginkgo'?Tucked between two mountains, Buam-dong is recommended by travellers and locals for its picturesque views, art galleries and cosy cafes - an escape from Seoul's bustle.Because of its proximity to the Blue House, the president's official residence, urban development has been restricted, allowing the neighbourhood to retain its quaint charm.In a place where you usually find ginkgo trees in private gardens or untamed forests, this one is special, Jung says, because it flourished on the side of the road. To her, it's "Grandpa Ginkgo"."I pass this tree whenever I come home. I would say, 'Grandpa, I'm home.' Or 'Grandpa, I'm heading out now'." Jung only moved here four years ago, but the grand old tree was the first thing she noticed, and she grew to love it."It was the only tree in the neighbourhood that belongs to everyone."To Park Jeon-hee, who has lived here for nearly all his 74 years, the ginkgo is his "oldest friend". It's the same for 10-year-old Kim On, who walks past it every day on his way to school. It has stood since before he was born, Kim says, and "thinking it might fall down makes me sad".Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Buam-dong is popular among people looking for an escape from Seoul's busy centreSo it wasn't surprising that Jung found ready allies in the community who had also noticed the ginkgo's withering leaves.They soon became suspicious of 10 white plastic funnels peeping out from behind the trunk. Jung had initially assumed they were providing nutrients, but then began to wonder if something more sinister was at play.She and her neighbours sieved through security camera footage from a nearby house, until they found something odd: one morning in late April, the camera had recorded two men wearing white gloves and crouching over the base of the tree with a drill.Were these men installing the funnels? Jung and the others couldn't exactly tell from the footage.But then they remembered something the local council had told them: a museum had previously asked landowners in the area for permission to remove the tree.The Whanki Museum had apparently claimed that its outer brick wall, which sits inches from the ginkgo, was under strain from the tree's roots.The residents soon suspected the funnels contained some kind of herbicide that was slowly killing the tree - a suspicion also shared by arborists who came to examine it. And they believed the Whanki Museum was behind it all.On the very day they saw the footage, a group of Buam-dong residents stormed into the museum, accompanied by four police officers. When confronted, an employee "basically admitted" the museum had done something to the tree, Jung and her neighbour alleged."Once they had said it, there was really no taking it back," the neighbour told the BBC.The museum has neither publicly confirmed nor denied injecting herbicide into the tree, and has not responded to the BBC's questions.But it did publish a statement in May, saying the wall of its compound was "collapsing because of the ginkgo's roots". It said it had sent letters to more than 40 property owners "requesting a solution".There was no response, the museum said, so its staff "attempted to resolve the situation". It did not explain what they had done.A local council representative told the BBC that an inspection last year found "no meaningful connection" between the ginkgo tree and damage to the museum wall. If there had been an issue, "we would have taken appropriate action and informed the relevant parties," the official added.The residents, who still believe the Whanki Museum had the funnels installed, want them to reveal what was in them, so experts can treat the ginkgo. They have filed a police report against the museum's director. Officials say police are investigating the case, but police declined to share more information when contacted by the BBC.Image source, Seoul KFEMImage caption, Residents allege that the Whanki Museum has poisoned the ginkgo tree'In the hands of heaven'Opened in 1992, the museum is dedicated to the late Kim Whanki, a celebrated painter and abstract artist, known by many as the "Picasso of Korea".On the museum website, architect Woo Kyusung explains he wanted to create a space for Kim's works "that would complement the elements of the nature - the moon, mountains, clouds, rocks and trees - that were so important to his art".In fact, Kim wrote essays under the pen name Su-wha, which translates to "conversation with trees".The irony is not lost on Buam-dong's indignant residents. Decades after Kim's death, the museum built in his honour is accused of trying to snuff out a tree. A ginkgo, no less, which is precious in Korea, where it symbolises longevity and resilience."Treating life that way is ignorance and there was never any apology," Jung says.The residents have co-opted Kim's poetic nom de plume "Su-wha" for their moribund tree. They have also roped in an environmental activist group, which has launched a petition calling for citizens to be authorised as guardians of urban trees."When I first heard that a tree next to a museum had been poisoned with herbicide and was dying, I simply couldn't believe it," says activist Choi Jin-woo. But when he saw the ginkgo shrivelling, he "realised something this horrific could actually happen in our society".Image source, Yujin Choi/BBCImage caption, The Whanki Museum is dedicated to a pioneering artist known by many as the "Picasso of Korea"If there's a silver lining to be found in the ginkgo's troubles, it's that the campaign to keep it alive has brought the people of Buam-dong closer together.While spending her days garnering support, Jung would return to find home-cooked meals from her neighbours left by her door. She, in turn, made vegetable soup for neighbours she'd never met before.As summer went by, they all watched the ginkgo's branches increasingly go bare and brown. An arborist who inspected it said it was "90% of the way toward death", Choi says.The fate of the tree is now "in the hands of heaven", says a resigned Jung. "Perhaps all I can do is stay beside it and pray."For weeks, around 20 residents regularly gathered in front of the tree to pray for its recovery. Some recited Whanki's essays, while a local shaman performed a "healing ritual".Image source, Yujin Choi/BBCImage caption, Residents perform an "elm dance", which they believe promotes ecological healingNotes of well wishes fluttered against the trunk as music rang out, and the group joined hands and swayed in unison for an "elm dance", which some nature lovers and activists believe helps trees heal."If someone had truly understood this tree was deeply loved, they probably would not have made the decision to inject herbicide," says Kim Min-joo, who has lived in Buam-dong for more than a decade.Image source, Yujin Choi/BBCImage caption, Residents gathered regularly in front of the ginkgo tree to pray for its recoveryIt recently occurred to Jung that all the days that she spent scrambling to save the ginkgo were the most active she had been since she fell ill last winter.She had struggled to walk much and would often observe the tree from home. On better days, she strolled up to it, even hugging its jagged trunk and inhaling the earthy scent to lift her spirits. "I felt so depressed and hopeless but those feelings disappeared. I entered a tree-like state."She still can't walk very much, she adds, but "the tree helped bring me back out into life again. Ironically, it was because the tree became sick.""Although it has been heartbreaking, there were also incredibly moving moments," Jung says, on reflection. "The neighbourhood came together, cared for one another, looked after each other."As Seoul transforms into various shades of yellow with the arrival of autumn, the leaves on Buam-dong's once-prized ginkgo are a crispy brown.The neighbourhood is still hoping for a miracle. They cannot imagine an autumn in which they don't pause to admire the ginkgo at its finest, swathed in a feathery coat of gold.Image source, Yujin Choi/BBCSeoulSouth KoreaNature

schema.headline: When a beloved tree began withering away, locals suspected a killer in their midst
